title: The metta sutta
hookLine: the discourse on kindness: as a mother protects her only child

lines: A MOTHER AND HER ONLY CHILD.
cards: Ten short verses in Pali, about two minutes read aloud. In Theravada temples, from Sri Lanka to Thailand, monks chant them as a protective text, and lay people learn them by heart.
It's the Karaniya Metta Sutta, the discourse on loving-kindness. You've already met pieces of it, in the wishes for all beings. Today you get the whole thing.
And at its center is a single picture: a mother, and her only child.

teach.b: The sutta begins with its own first word: karaniya. It means what should be done. This is what should be done, it says, by someone skilled in the good.
Then it describes the kind of person who practices metta. Capable. Upright.
Easy to talk to. Gentle, not proud. Content, living simply, not burdened with too many duties.
It starts with how you live, before it talks about how you feel. Then come the wishes: may all beings be happy and secure, may their hearts be glad.

teach.h: THE WEAK AND THE STRONG, SEEN AND UNSEEN.
teach.b: The weak and the strong, the long and the short, the seen and the unseen, near and far, born and still to be born. Let no one deceive another, or despise anyone anywhere, or wish harm on anyone in anger.

And then the image. As a mother would protect her only child, even at the risk of her own life, so, the sutta says, one should cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings. That isn't a mild good wish.
It's a mother's fierce, total, protective love for her only child, spread to everyone, without limit.
Standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as you're awake, keep this mindfulness.
The commentary tells how it began: monks meditating in a forest were frightened by spirits, and the Buddha gave them this to recite, so they went back with kindness instead of fear.
Yourself, a benefactor, a friend, a stranger, a difficult person, no barriers, all beings: you've practiced each piece, and the sutta holds all of it in ten verses.

how: Theravada Buddhists chant the Karaniya Metta Sutta in Pali, at home or at ceremonies, as one of the protective chants (paritta), and it is often learned by heart.

games.q: you're a monk meditating in a forest, and the spirits there frighten you. what does the commentary say the Buddha gave you?
o: a charm to drive them away.
the Metta Sutta, to recite with kindness.
games.why: the commentary says he taught them this sutta, and they returned to the forest with kindness instead of fear.

practice: Bring to mind the fiercest protective love you've ever felt or received: a parent for a child, someone for a pet, a friend in an emergency.
Keeping its strength, let that same care widen slowly, like ripples, to the people nearest you, then your street, your city, then everywhere. May all beings be happy and secure.

wordCard.voice: Karaniya. What should be done: the first word of the discourse on loving-kindness, and the name people know it by.

orig.note: Pali: what should be done; the sutta's first word and its name.

carryVoice: Your line: as a mother. Day one hundred and five, and a week of metta, done.
